Brazilian officials first raised concerns with Apple nearly three months ago about minors' access to gambling apps, and Apple has now been given a five-working-day deadline to provide further information on the safeguards in its App Store. Details of the case are below.

Apple faces regulatory and age-verification pressure

In April of last year, Brazilian officials sent separate notices to Apple and Google, alleging that the two companies' app stores lacked age restrictions for gambling apps.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) each wrote to the two companies, asking whether "countless apps" were offering or facilitating minors' access to gambling platforms.

Brazil recently passed a new law called the Children and Adolescents Digital Law (ECA Digital Law), which requires app stores to restrict minors' access to gambling content. Apple subsequently introduced age-verification measures for 18-rated apps in the country.

However, officials said that, based on preliminary investigations, many gambling apps appeared to lack appropriate age restrictions or federal authorisation, raising doubts about the effectiveness of current safeguards.

Although Apple's full response has not been made fully public, the relevant departments have now said that Apple has answered most of their initial questions and the authorities are still requesting further information.

Quoted from Brazil's Ministry of Justice and Public Security (via Canaltech):

The authorities' requests for clarification include: how apps listed in Brazil verify regulatory authorisation; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulated apps from those involving real-money gambling, including cases where approved features are subsequently hidden or altered; and mechanisms to prevent minors' access to inappropriate content. The authorities also requested information on proactive monitoring procedures, risk-prioritisation criteria, average takedown times, and a timeline for publishing the implementation of remedial measures—including software update design.

The two secretariats noted that Google's response fell short of expectations and requested more detailed information on: how the company verifies authorised operators, how it monitors apps whose licences have been revoked or have expired, how it measures enforcement effectiveness, and how it prevents minors from searching for or downloading gambling apps.

Finally, the two secretariats requested that Apple's and Google's responses be made public, though confidential information could be submitted separately on a restricted-access basis.
